vignette: Nora, a 68-year-old prison guard of Middle Eastern descent, had always taken pride in her ability to keep others safe. However, the sense of control and protection she once felt shattered one night during a routine shift at the prison. It was late when a violent altercation broke out between two inmates. Nora rushed to intervene, but in the chaos, one of the men turned on her, striking her in the face. The assault left her physically bruised but, more devastatingly, it fractured her sense of self-worth and security. In the months that followed, Nora found herself grappling with a profound feeling of failure; she believed she should have been able to protect not only herself but also the inmates she was responsible for. This belief of having failed to protect others haunted her, solidifying a negative appraisal that she was now an outsider, someone who could no longer be trusted to fulfill her role effectively. Convinced that she was unworthy and incapable, Nora adopted maladaptive strategies to cope with these feelings, believing that if she could prove her worth through relentless work, she might overcome this perceived failure. In her mind, if she was incapable of protecting those under her care, then any attempt to engage with her responsibilities felt futile, leading her to adopt strategies that would keep her busy, as a way to compensate for her perceived inadequacies. In her mind, the only way to regain some semblance of control was to keep herself busy, believing that if she could prove her worth through relentless work, she might overcome this perceived failure. Convinced that she was incapable and unworthy, Nora began to employ maladaptive strategies to cope with her feelings of inadequacy, thinking that if she stayed busy and engaged, perhaps she could prove her worth once more. Convinced that her failure defined her worth, she sought to compensate for her perceived inadequacies through maladaptive strategies, believing that staying busy would somehow prove she was still capable. The aftermath of the assault transformed her daily life into a constant state of vigilance. Nora began to monitor her environment obsessively, scanning for any signs of danger wherever she went. Her heightened sense of threat made her feel as though any moment could lead to chaos, compelling her to adopt these vigilance strategies as a means of self-protection. When the threat felt this close, meticulously checking her surroundings and planning her exits was not just a symptom of anxiety; it was the only rational thing to do to ensure her safety. When danger seemed imminent, it made perfect sense to her that she should meticulously check her surroundings and plan her exits, believing these actions were essential for her safety. Even in familiar places, like her own home, she felt an overwhelming urge to check every corner and doorway, her body reacting to perceived threats before her mind could catch up. The silence of her living room, once a comforting respite, now felt ominous, as if it were a prelude to something dangerous lurking just out of sight. This hyper-vigilance extended to her sleep patterns; she struggled to fall asleep, her mind racing with thoughts of potential dangers, both real and imagined. The longer she went without adequate rest, the more her sense of alertness heightened, feeding into her fears and solidifying her belief that danger was an ever-present reality. This constant state of alertness reinforced her negative appraisal that she had become vulnerable and incapable, further entrenching the idea that she could not be trusted to navigate her environment safely. To cope with these overwhelming feelings, Nora sought solace in social situations, surrounding herself with friends and family almost constantly. She thought that by staying busy and engaged with others, she could avoid confronting her thoughts and feelings, which only compounded her negative beliefs about herself. The irony was not lost on her; in her effort to avoid being alone with her thoughts, she often dropped important responsibilities both at work and at home. Each time she avoided confronting her feelings by immersing herself in social situations, it only reinforced her negative beliefs, whispering to her that she was fragile and unable to cope with her responsibilities. She felt that her reliance on these avoidance behaviors only confirmed her belief that she was incapable of managing her life, as each instance of retreating deepened her sense of failure. Each time she retreated into these avoidance behaviors, Nora felt a quiet confirmation of her fears - that her struggles were valid and that the threats she perceived were real and ongoing, further deepening her sense of danger. Each time she engaged in these avoidance behaviors, she felt a quiet confirmation of her fears - that she was fragile and incapable of managing her life, deepening her negative self-assessment. Tasks that had once been manageable now seemed insurmountable, leading her to feel even more like an outsider in her own life. Each time she withdrew from her responsibilities, a new wave of guilt washed over her, reinforcing the belief that she was failing those who depended on her, thus tightening the cycle of avoidance and self-recrimination. As the months turned into years, Nora's life became increasingly defined by her fear of the world around her. The constant socializing that had once offered her comfort began to feel like a cage, imprisoning her in her own mind. She was aware, on some level, that her strategies were maladaptive, yet they felt like her only means of survival in a world that had become terrifyingly unpredictable. The mistrust she felt towards others deepened; she couldn't shake the feeling that anyone could be a potential threat, that people simply couldn't be trusted. This pervasive mistrust not only alienated her from those she cared about but also eroded her ability to connect with her colleagues at work, making her feel more isolated than ever. The more she isolated herself, the less she tested her fears, which meant she never allowed herself to see that the threats she perceived might not be as real as her body insisted they were. Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed - the threat remained as high as the day it was set. By continuously avoiding her triggers, she inadvertently fortified her sense of threat, as she never encountered situations that could demonstrate her ability to feel safe again. The more she relied on her maladaptive strategies to navigate her fears, the more her body interpreted those actions as validation of real and ongoing danger, perpetuating her heightened sense of threat. Nora's journey brought her to the point where she realized she could no longer manage on her own. The accumulation of sleepless nights, the relentless scanning for danger, and the heavy burden of guilt had become too much to bear. In her heart, she hoped for relief from the perpetual anxiety that gripped her, but fear also loomed large in her mind. She was terrified that confronting her trauma would only confirm her worst fears-that she was irrevocably broken, incapable of ever feeling secure or safe again. This fear was compounded by the idea that acknowledging her trauma might expose her to the reality of her ongoing threat perception, a truth she was desperate to avoid. This unrelenting sense of threat was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair, leading her to view herself as someone who could no longer feel safe in any situation. Yet, the glimmer of hope that perhaps understanding her pain could lead her to reclaim her life compelled her to seek help. It was a tentative step, but for Nora, it felt like the first move toward healing.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not establish how Nora's negative appraisals of herself drive her to engage in maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette fails to connect Nora's sense of threat to her negative appraisals about her self-worth.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not demonstrate how Nora's maladaptive strategies reinforce her negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette lacks a connection between Nora's maladaptive strategies and her perception of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

vignette_attempts.vignette: Nora, a 68-year-old prison guard of Middle Eastern descent, had always taken pride in her ability to keep others safe. However, the sense of control and protection she once felt shattered one night during a routine shift at the prison. It was late when a violent altercation broke out between two inmates. Nora rushed to intervene, but in the chaos, one of the men turned on her, striking her in the face. The assault left her physically bruised but, more devastatingly, it fractured her sense of self-worth and security. In the months that followed, Nora found herself grappling with a profound feeling of failure; she believed she should have been able to protect not only herself but also the inmates she was responsible for. This belief of having failed to protect others haunted her, solidifying a negative appraisal that she was now an outsider, someone who could no longer be trusted to fulfill her role effectively. In her mind, if she was incapable of protecting those under her care, then any attempt to engage with her responsibilities felt futile, leading her to adopt strategies that would keep her busy, as a way to compensate for her perceived inadequacies. In her mind, the only way to regain some semblance of control was to keep herself busy, believing that if she could prove her worth through relentless work, she might overcome this perceived failure. Convinced that she was incapable and unworthy, Nora began to employ maladaptive strategies to cope with her feelings of inadequacy, thinking that if she stayed busy and engaged, perhaps she could prove her worth once more. Convinced that her failure defined her worth, she sought to compensate for her perceived inadequacies through maladaptive strategies, believing that staying busy would somehow prove she was still capable. The aftermath of the assault transformed her daily life into a constant state of vigilance. Nora began to monitor her environment obsessively, scanning for any signs of danger wherever she went. Her heightened sense of threat made her feel as though any moment could lead to chaos, compelling her to adopt these vigilance strategies as a means of self-protection. When danger seemed imminent, it made perfect sense to her that she should meticulously check her surroundings and plan her exits, believing these actions were essential for her safety. Even in familiar places, like her own home, she felt an overwhelming urge to check every corner and doorway, her body reacting to perceived threats before her mind could catch up. The silence of her living room, once a comforting respite, now felt ominous, as if it were a prelude to something dangerous lurking just out of sight. This hyper-vigilance extended to her sleep patterns; she struggled to fall asleep, her mind racing with thoughts of potential dangers, both real and imagined. The longer she went without adequate rest, the more her sense of alertness heightened, feeding into her fears and solidifying her belief that danger was an ever-present reality. This constant state of alertness reinforced her negative appraisal that she had become vulnerable and incapable, further entrenching the idea that she could not be trusted to navigate her environment safely. To cope with these overwhelming feelings, Nora sought solace in social situations, surrounding herself with friends and family almost constantly. She thought that by staying busy and engaged with others, she could avoid confronting her thoughts and feelings, which only compounded her negative beliefs about herself. The irony was not lost on her; in her effort to avoid being alone with her thoughts, she often dropped important responsibilities both at work and at home. Each time she avoided confronting her feelings by immersing herself in social situations, it only reinforced her negative beliefs, whispering to her that she was fragile and unable to cope with her responsibilities. She felt that her reliance on these avoidance behaviors only confirmed her belief that she was incapable of managing her life, as each instance of retreating deepened her sense of failure. Each time she retreated into these avoidance behaviors, Nora felt a quiet confirmation of her fears — that her struggles were valid and that the threats she perceived were real and ongoing, further deepening her sense of danger. Each time she engaged in these avoidance behaviors, she felt a quiet confirmation of her fears — that she was fragile and incapable of managing her life, deepening her negative self-assessment. Tasks that had once been manageable now seemed insurmountable, leading her to feel even more like an outsider in her own life. Each time she withdrew from her responsibilities, a new wave of guilt washed over her, reinforcing the belief that she was failing those who depended on her, thus tightening the cycle of avoidance and self-recrimination. As the months turned into years, Nora’s life became increasingly defined by her fear of the world around her. The constant socializing that had once offered her comfort began to feel like a cage, imprisoning her in her own mind. She was aware, on some level, that her strategies were maladaptive, yet they felt like her only means of survival in a world that had become terrifyingly unpredictable. The mistrust she felt towards others deepened; she couldn’t shake the feeling that anyone could be a potential threat, that people simply couldn’t be trusted. This pervasive mistrust not only alienated her from those she cared about but also eroded her ability to connect with her colleagues at work, making her feel more isolated than ever. The more she isolated herself, the less she tested her fears, which meant she never allowed herself to see that the threats she perceived might not be as real as her body insisted they were. In her heart, she hoped for relief from the perpetual anxiety that gripped her, but fear also loomed large in her mind. She was terrified that confronting her trauma would only confirm her worst fears—that she was irrevocably broken, incapable of ever feeling secure or safe again. This fear was compounded by the idea that acknowledging her trauma might expose her to the reality of her ongoing threat perception, a truth she was desperate to avoid. This unrelenting sense of threat was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair, leading her to view herself as someone who could no longer feel safe in any situation. Yet, the glimmer of hope that perhaps understanding her pain could lead her to reclaim her life compelled her to seek help.
